platforms.title: Why Does Sudden Hearing Loss Need Same-Day Care?
platforms.meta_description: One ear stops working almost overnight? Sudden sensorineural hearing loss is a real emergency, and how fast you're treated can change your odds of recovery.
platforms.body_html:
If one ear suddenly feels muffled or stops picking up sound the way it did yesterday, it's tempting to blame earwax or a cold and wait a few days to see if it clears up. With sudden sensorineural hearing loss (SSNHL), that wait can cost you the window when treatment actually works. SSNHL is a drop of at least 30 decibels across three connected frequencies, happening within 72 hours or less, usually in one ear — and hearing specialists treat it as an ear emergency, not a symptom to watch.

Why It Happens — Even When No Single Cause Is Found

According to the National Institute on Deafness and Other Communication Disorders (NIDCD), a specific cause is identified in only about 10 to 15 percent of cases — the rest are labeled idiopathic. Among the leading hypotheses researchers point to are a viral infection affecting the inner ear and a temporary disruption of blood flow to the cochlea, the organ that turns sound into nerve signals. Chronic stress and poor sleep don't directly cause SSNHL, but they're linked to autonomic nervous system strain that can affect blood flow throughout the body, including small vessels feeding the inner ear — one reason clinicians ask about recent stress and illness when SSNHL is diagnosed.

Separately, long-term noise exposure is one of the best-documented, modifiable risks to hearing in general. It doesn't need to trigger a sudden episode to matter — cumulative damage to the hair cells inside the cochlea from loud, prolonged sound reduces your overall hearing reserve over years, and it's entirely within your control.

The Treatment Window the Guidelines Actually Point To

The American Academy of Otolaryngology–Head and Neck Surgery's 2019 clinical practice guideline update recommends that clinicians offer corticosteroid treatment — oral or injected directly into the ear — within two weeks of symptom onset, since that's the window where the evidence for benefit is strongest. Intratympanic (in-ear) steroid injections are specifically recommended as salvage therapy when hearing hasn't recovered two to six weeks after the initial episode, and hyperbaric oxygen therapy combined with steroids can also be offered within that early period. Outcomes vary widely by individual, but across the research, earlier treatment is consistently associated with a better chance of meaningful hearing recovery than treatment started weeks later.

Cut the Delay Before It Costs You

  • Treat sudden one-sided hearing change as urgent — same-day or next-day audiology or ENT evaluation, not a wait-and-see approach, especially if it's paired with ringing or dizziness.
  • Use the 60/60 habit with headphones — Mayo Clinic audiologists popularized this rule of thumb, as an easy proxy for WHO safe-listening guidance on cumulative noise exposure: keep volume at or below 60 percent of maximum and take a break after about 60 minutes of continuous listening.
  • Don't skip sleep and recovery when you're run down — it won't prevent every case, but supporting your body's stress response is a reasonable, low-cost habit alongside everything else.
  • Ask specifically about steroid treatment timing if you're diagnosed with SSNHL — the two-week window is the detail worth confirming with your clinician, not just whether treatment is available.

None of this guarantees a full recovery, since SSNHL outcomes depend on factors doctors can't always control. But the single detail worth remembering is timing: a hearing change that happens overnight deserves a same-day phone call, not a few days of waiting to see if it passes on its own.
